title: What If a Surgeon Removed Your Whole Stomach? People Live Without One

scenes.text: What if a surgeon removed your whole stomach? Thousands live without one. They still eat dinner.
In a total gastrectomy the oesophagus is stitched straight to the small intestine. The hospital stay can run two weeks.
scenes.keywords: anatomy model digestive system hospital bed

scenes.text: Healing takes six to eight weeks. Then three big meals become six small ones, eaten slowly, for life.
Without a stomach you can't absorb vitamin B12, so many patients get an injection every month, forever.
Food rushing into the intestine causes dumping syndrome. Many people lose around 10 percent of their body weight.
Some choose it before any cancer appears. Carriers of the CDH1 gene face roughly a 40 percent lifetime risk of stomach cancer.

description:
What if your whole stomach were removed? After a total gastrectomy the oesophagus is joined directly to the small intestine; recovery takes about six to eight weeks, meals become six small ones a day, and vitamin B12 usually has to be injected because it can no longer be absorbed.
Many patients lose around 10 percent of their body weight. The operation is done for stomach cancer and preventively for carriers of a CDH1 gene mutation, whose lifetime risk is roughly 40 percent. Information only, not medical advice.

first_comment: The stomach mostly stores and churns food; the real digestion happens in the intestine, which is why you can live without it. Which organ do you think you could spare? And what should we run through next?
